extracted.subtask_description: Measuring and comparing the volume, complexity, and targeting of state-level administrative regulation using quantitative text-analysis metrics (RegData) applied to state administrative codes, with complementary population- and industry-based adjustments. The brief applies these metrics to four states and DC in the Mideast BEA region as an illustrative snapshot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory restriction (primary unit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary unit of measurement of regulation in RegData is the regulatory restriction, or instance of the terms shall, must, may not, prohibited, and required appearing in administrative laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms approximate the restrictions that regulators impose on a jurisdiction; counting instances of these terms produces an estimate of restrictiveness. Use this definition consistently when comparing across jurisdictions. Be aware that this is an approximation of regulatory burden based on lexical signals rather than a direct measure of substantive impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of words in administrative code (word count)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the words in each state's administrative code to compare the size of regulatory codes (e.g., New York Codes, Rules, and Regulations contains over 17.6 million words; Delaware Administrative Code contains 5.9 million words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is perhaps the simplest way to compare states’ regulatory environments. Word count gives a measure of regulatory volume but does not directly measure restrictiveness, complexity, or economic impact—interpret alongside other metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of regulatory restrictions (restrictive-term counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count occurrences of restrictive terms (see 'regulatory restriction' definition) in administrative codes to produce a quantitative measure of how regulated a jurisdiction is (e.g., New York: 296,296 restrictions; Delaware: 93,421).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an estimate of regulatory restrictiveness. Use for cross-state comparisons but consider differences in drafting style, scope of codes, and enforcement practice which can affect raw counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity of regulatory text (Shannon Entropy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the complexity of regulatory text using Shannon Entropy from information theory: higher entropy implies content spans a wider range of topics and is more complex; lower entropy implies easier-to-read documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no standard interpretation of magnitude; generally, higher Shannon Entropy suggests more mental bandwidth required to understand and potentially higher compliance costs. Use reference points (the brief notes Shakespeare plays ~9.0–9.8) and compare relatively across jurisdictions. Report entropy alongside examples and caution against overinterpreting absolute values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-targeted regulatory restrictions (RegData industry mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use machine learning algorithms trained to identify text relevant to particular industries; combine the probability that text applies to an industry with restriction counts to estimate the number of regulatory restrictions targeting particular sectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields per-industry restriction estimates and allows comparison of which industries are most regulated within and across states. Be explicit about the ML model, its training, and probability thresholds. Understand that estimates depend on model accuracy and the choice of industries/categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of most-regulated industries (top-N inclusion rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the five most regulated industries by estimated restriction count for each state, and when aggregating across states present a consistent set of industries (the brief shows 14 industries across states because some industries appear in multiple states' top-five lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing comparative figures, include a common industry set across jurisdictions (even if an industry is not top-five in a given state) to enable cross-state comparisons. Document selection rules and any data omissions (e.g., BEA data gaps such as exclusion of food and beverage stores in some figures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualizing industry restrictions with GDP contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the percentage of state GDP associated with each industry alongside restriction counts to contextualize how regulatory targeting relates to economic importance (e.g., real estate is a major GDP contributor but tends to be less regulated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume causal relationships between restriction volume and GDP contribution; present both metrics to inform interpretation. Use weighted analyses when assessing federal regulation impact (see FRASE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Regulation and State Enterprise (FRASE) index
rubrics_metrics.description: An index that weights estimates of industry-relevant federal restrictions according to how important various industries are to state GDP to rank states on how regulated they are by the federal government (scaled relative to the nation; e.g., Pennsylvania 1.01 in 2017 means 1% more targeted than the national average).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use FRASE to compare the degree to which federal regulation targets states' economies. Clearly state the weighting method, base year scaling, and interpretation of index values (values relative to 1.00). Combine with state-level restriction counts for a fuller picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population-adjusted restriction counts (restrictions per capita)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust restriction counts for population (e.g., restrictions per 1,000 residents) to account for population differences across states (e.g., DC: 194.4 restrictions per 1,000 residents; Pennsylvania: 12.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjusting for population can reveal different rankings than raw counts and helps account for fixed regulatory costs and population-driven regulatory scope. Also report GDP per capita or other economic context because richer jurisdictions may both have more regulations and higher GDP per capita; avoid inferring causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing state vs federal volumes (absolute-count comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare aggregate counts of state regulatory restrictions with federal restrictions to gauge relative scale (e.g., average for these states ~162,661 restrictions vs ~1.09 million in the Code of Federal Regulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use absolute comparisons to understand the potential relative impact of federal versus state regulation on local economies. Recognize the difference in scope and jurisdiction—federal rules may affect states differently depending on industry composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: RegData methodological approach (text analysis and ML to quantify legal text)
rubrics_metrics.description: RegData converts legal text into quantitative data using text analysis and machine learning algorithms to quantify regulation in a jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying RegData methods, document preprocessing, lexicon choices (e.g., restrictive-term list), ML model details, validation, and limitations. Be transparent about data versions (the brief uses State RegData version 2.1) and any jurisdictional data gaps (e.g., New Jersey excluded due to data availability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats and multi-metric interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each metric (word counts, restriction counts, entropy, industry targeting, per-capita adjustments, FRASE) has its own advantages and disadvantages; use multiple complementary metrics and avoid overreliance on any single measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state limitations, do not assume causality between regulation volume and economic outcomes, cross-validate findings, and pursue further research to understand temporal evolution and consequences. Present results as a 'snapshot' and contextualize with qualitative knowledge of drafting practices and enforcement.
